summary: This is an April 1st joke RFC that adapts RFC 1149, which describes sending IP datagrams by carrier pigeon, to IPv6. It is humorous, not a real protocol, though it is written in the style of a serious one.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6214 is an April 1st joke document about adapting the RFC 1149 avian-carrier medium to IPv6. It applies IPv6 terms to that imaginary setting and is not an Internet Standards Track specification.

subtitle: An April 1st joke document that adapts the avian-carrier specification to IPv6.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke document imagines how providers using the RFC 1149 medium could carry IPv6 datagrams.
tldr.mechanism: It applies IPv6 requirements to the avian-carrier medium and discusses packet size, framing, addressing, service classes, routing and security in deadpan technical language.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational joke document and explicitly says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.

today: RFC 6214 is an Informational April 1st joke document that updates RFC 1149; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It is explicitly not a candidate for any Internet Standard.

sections.title: An April 1st IPv6 Adaptation
sections.content:
RFC 6214 is an April 1st joke document that adapts RFC 1149, the specification for carrying IP datagrams on avian carriers, to IPv6. Its introduction says the goal is to let providers keep the same medium while moving from IPv4 to IPv6.

The RFC says that, unless otherwise stated, provisions of RFC 1149 and RFC 2460 apply. It is published for informational purposes and is not a candidate for any Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st document applies IPv6 rules to the avian-carrier medium from RFC 1149. It is a joke specification, not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Packet Size and Frame Format
sections.content:
The text says RFC 1149's maximum transmission unit (MTU) varies with carrier age. Since IPv6 requires a minimum link MTU of 1280 octets, the document concludes that older carriers must be used. It gives an illustrative calculation using 256 milligrams as 576 octets, producing about 569 milligrams and an example age of at least 365 days.

It specifies a pure IPv6 packet without a link-layer tag. In a dual-stack setup, a receiver must inspect the first four bits to distinguish IPv4 and IPv6 packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke applies IPv6's minimum packet-size requirement to the RFC 1149 carrier. It also says a receiver must inspect the packet version to tell IPv4 from IPv6.

sections.title: Addressing, Multicast and Service Classes
sections.content:
The RFC says the medium has no link-layer protocol, so link-local addresses and Neighbor Discovery cannot be used. It advises against stateless address autoconfiguration and says endpoints may remain unnumbered or use static addresses with a /127 prefix. It specifies no IPv6 multicast mapping.

For non-default Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) values, packets must be marked in green or blue ink, not red. This section applies quality-of-service concepts from the cited RFCs to the joke's carrier setting.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says the medium cannot use several normal IPv6 address and discovery methods. It also gives ink-color rules for packets with special service markings.

sections.title: Routing and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes routing problems involving carriers crossing territories, including loops, out-of-order delivery and packet loss. It recommends considering policy-based routing. It also jokes about carriers eating other carriers as a possible tunnel and says the decapsulation method is unclear.

It says these carriers cannot support multihoming without routing loops. Its security section mentions denial-of-service risks, the lack of link-layer identifiers and checksums, and the need for upper-layer security. It also requires detection and quarantine measures for the H5N1 virus.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC applies routing and security concerns to its fictional carrier network. It uses these examples to continue the joke while discussing real networking terms.
